def: A germ cell tumor containing tissue from all three germ layers, often hair, teeth, bone or cartilage. Mature cystic forms in the ovary are benign (dermoid cyst); immature forms contain primitive neuroepithelium and are malignant.
The earliest extraembryonic membrane. In humans it supports early blood cell formation and gives rise to primordial germ cells; its remnant in the gut can persist as a Meckel diverticulum.
A lymphoma arising from malignant B lymphocytes, including diffuse large B-cell, follicular, Burkitt and mantle cell types. Tumor cells typically express CD19 and CD20.

Failures of the neural tube to close in early embryogenesis, producing anencephaly, spina bifida or encephalocele. Risk falls with folic acid before conception; maternal serum alpha-fetoprotein is elevated.

Glucose intolerance first recognized during pregnancy, caused by placental hormones (such as human placental lactogen) that increase insulin resistance. It raises the risk of macrosomia and later type 2 diabetes.

A chronic autoimmune disease with anti-nuclear, anti-dsDNA and anti-Smith antibodies and immune-complex deposition. It causes malar rash, arthritis, serositis, nephritis and cytopenias, most often in young women.
New, highly vascular connective tissue of capillaries and fibroblasts that fills a wound during healing. It is replaced by collagenous scar and appears red and granular.

An autosomal recessive defect of the ATP7B copper transporter that blocks biliary copper excretion. Copper builds up in liver, basal ganglia and cornea, causing cirrhosis, movement disorders and Kayser-Fleischer rings.
Defective mineralization of growing bone in children, usually from vitamin D deficiency. It causes bowed legs, widened growth plates and costochondral beading (rachitic rosary).

The low-pressure circuit carrying deoxygenated blood from the right ventricle through the lungs and back to the left atrium as oxygenated blood. Hypoxia constricts its vessels, unlike in systemic vessels.

The central compartment of the chest between the two pleural cavities, containing the heart, great vessels, trachea, esophagus, thymus and lymph nodes. It is divided into superior, anterior, middle and posterior parts.

A signaling protein that drives new blood vessel growth (angiogenesis) and raises vascular permeability. It is induced by hypoxia and is the target of bevacizumab in cancer and ranibizumab in wet macular degeneration.

Repeated collapse of the upper airway during sleep, causing apneas, snoring and daytime sleepiness. It is associated with obesity and can lead to hypertension, pulmonary hypertension and polycythemia.
The amide form of niacin (vitamin B3), a precursor of NAD and NADP used in redox reactions. Deficiency causes pellagra with dermatitis, diarrhea and dementia.
Thin nasal discharge, seen with viral rhinitis or allergy. Clear watery fluid after head trauma suggests a cerebrospinal fluid leak from a skull base fracture.
A form of COPD defined by productive cough on most days for at least 3 months in 2 consecutive years. It is caused mainly by smoking and shows mucus gland hypertrophy (increased Reid index).
A pruritic inflammatory skin condition with red, scaly, weeping or lichenified patches. Atopic dermatitis, linked to atopy and filaggrin mutations, is the classic form in children.

Infection by Aspergillus, a mold with septate hyphae branching at acute angles. It causes allergic bronchopulmonary disease, fungus balls in old cavities, and invasive pulmonary disease in neutropenic patients.

Lung infection after inhaling oral or gastric contents, usually with anaerobes and oral flora. It favors the right lower lobe or posterior upper lobes in recumbent patients, often with impaired swallowing or consciousness.
A normal gene that promotes cell growth and division. Gain-of-function mutation, amplification or translocation turns it into an oncogene, such as RAS, MYC or HER2.
Transient, itchy raised wheals from mast cell histamine release causing dermal edema. It is often IgE-mediated (type I hypersensitivity) and resolves within hours.
A neurodevelopmental disorder of inattention, hyperactivity and impulsivity beginning before age 12 and present in multiple settings. First-line treatment is stimulants such as methylphenidate.

A leukemia of malignant lymphoid cells. Acute lymphoblastic leukemia affects children with immature blasts, while chronic lymphocytic leukemia affects older adults with mature B cells and smudge cells.

An encapsulated yeast, Cryptococcus neoformans, spread from pigeon droppings and soil. It causes meningitis in immunocompromised patients, especially in AIDS, and appears with India ink as a halo around the yeast.
A mesh of sugar chains cross-linked by short peptides that forms the bacterial cell wall. It is thick in Gram-positive bacteria and is the target of beta-lactams and vancomycin.
Bleeding between the dura and arachnoid, from torn bridging veins after head trauma. It appears as a crescent-shaped collection on CT, and is common in the elderly and alcoholics.
Antidepressants that block reuptake of norepinephrine and serotonin. They also block muscarinic, H1 and alpha-1 receptors, and overdose causes arrhythmias, seizures and anticholinergic toxicity.
A protozoan that causes watery diarrhea by fecal-oral spread, often via contaminated water. It is self-limited in healthy people but chronic in AIDS, and oocysts are acid-fast.
Chronic infection by Mycobacterium leprae, which grows in cooler skin and nerves. It causes hypopigmented anesthetic skin lesions and neuropathy, in tuberculoid or lepromatous forms.
The main epidermal cells, which produce keratin and form the waterproof skin barrier. They mature upward through the stratum basale, spinosum, granulosum and corneum.
A Gq-coupled histamine receptor that mediates allergic responses: bronchoconstriction, vasodilation, increased vascular permeability and itch. It is blocked by antihistamines such as diphenhydramine.
A synthetic prostaglandin E1 analog. It keeps the ductus arteriosus open in newborns with ductal-dependent heart defects and treats erectile dysfunction by relaxing smooth muscle.
A diverse group of lymphoid cancers lacking Reed-Sternberg cells, mostly of B-cell origin. Examples include follicular, diffuse large B-cell, Burkitt and mantle cell lymphoma.
The thin layer of cells lining blood vessels and the heart. It regulates vascular tone with nitric oxide, controls permeability, and prevents clotting.
Ultrasound that uses frequency shifts of echoes from moving blood to measure flow speed and direction. It is used to detect stenosis, deep vein thrombosis and fetal blood flow.
A method that separates charged molecules such as proteins or DNA by their movement in an electric field. Serum protein electrophoresis detects monoclonal gammopathies as a spike.
A heart muscle disease with stiff, noncompliant ventricles that fill poorly in diastole while systolic function is preserved. Causes include amyloidosis, sarcoidosis, hemochromatosis and radiation.
The phase of the cardiac cycle when the ventricles relax and fill with blood. Coronary perfusion occurs mainly during this phase.

Backflow of blood from the right ventricle into the right atrium during systole, producing a holosystolic murmur that increases with inspiration. Causes include right ventricular dilation, endocarditis in drug users, and Ebstein anomaly.
Breathing too little to clear carbon dioxide, causing hypercapnia and respiratory acidosis. Causes include opioids, obesity hypoventilation and neuromuscular weakness; the A-a gradient stays normal.

Telescoping of one bowel segment into the next, causing obstruction and ischemia. It classically occurs in infants with colicky pain, currant jelly stool and a sausage-shaped mass, often at the ileocolic junction.
Inadequate blood flow to the intestines from arterial embolus, thrombosis or low flow. It causes severe abdominal pain out of proportion to exam and can progress to bowel infarction.
Heart attack from complete coronary occlusion causing transmural injury, shown by ST elevation on ECG and troponin release. Treatment is urgent reperfusion with percutaneous coronary intervention.
A non-enveloped double-stranded DNA virus causing pharyngitis, conjunctivitis, hemorrhagic cystitis and gastroenteritis. It spreads in close quarters such as military barracks.
Inflammation of the uvea (iris, ciliary body, choroid), causing eye pain, photophobia and a red eye. It is associated with HLA-B27 diseases, sarcoidosis and juvenile idiopathic arthritis.
A four-carbon intermediate of the citric acid cycle that combines with acetyl-CoA to form citrate. It is also made from pyruvate in gluconeogenesis and from aspartate by transamination.
Dendritic antigen-presenting cells of the epidermis. They carry Birbeck granules and are the cell of origin in Langerhans cell histiocytosis.
Elevated serum uric acid, from overproduction or underexcretion of purines. It can cause gout, uric acid kidney stones and tumor lysis syndrome complications.

Pyridoxine, whose active form pyridoxal phosphate is a cofactor in transamination, decarboxylation and heme synthesis. Deficiency (for example from isoniazid) causes neuropathy, sideroblastic anemia and seizures.
A high-energy intermediate formed from ammonia and bicarbonate by carbamoyl phosphate synthetase. It feeds the urea cycle (CPS I, mitochondria) and pyrimidine synthesis (CPS II, cytosol).
A lipid-rich insulating layer wrapped around axons, formed by oligodendrocytes in the CNS and Schwann cells in the PNS. It speeds conduction by saltatory jumps between nodes of Ranvier.
The formation of blood cells from stem cells. It occurs in the yolk sac, then liver and spleen in the fetus, then bone marrow after birth.

A group of disorders of heme synthesis in which porphyrin precursors accumulate. Acute intermittent porphyria causes abdominal pain and neuropsychiatric symptoms, while porphyria cutanea tarda causes blistering photosensitivity.
Reduced or absent beta-globin chain production, causing microcytic anemia. Severe forms (major) need transfusions and cause extramedullary hematopoiesis; HbA2 and HbF are increased.
The percentage of circulating immature red cells, reflecting marrow output. It is high with hemolysis or blood loss and low with marrow failure or nutritional deficiency.
A leukemia of mature, small B cells expressing CD5 and CD20, mainly in older adults. It shows lymphocytosis with fragile smudge cells and risks autoimmune hemolytic anemia.
The bundle of lumbar and sacral nerve roots below the end of the spinal cord (conus medullaris, about L1-L2). Compression causes saddle anesthesia, urinary retention and leg weakness.

A monosynaptic reflex in which muscle spindle stretch triggers contraction of the same muscle, as in the knee jerk. Absent reflexes suggest lower motor neuron disease, and brisk ones suggest upper motor neuron lesions.
An enveloped DNA virus causing oral lesions (cold sores) and encephalitis, usually temporal lobe. It stays latent in the trigeminal ganglion.
Impaired bile flow from the liver or through the bile ducts. It causes jaundice, pruritus, pale stool, dark urine and elevated alkaline phosphatase and conjugated bilirubin.
An enveloped, segmented negative-strand RNA virus family that includes influenza. Its hemagglutinin and neuraminidase proteins drive antigenic drift and shift.

A fluoroquinolone antibiotic that inhibits bacterial DNA gyrase and topoisomerase IV. It is active against Gram-negatives like Pseudomonas, and risks tendon rupture, QT prolongation and cartilage damage in children.
Anaerobic, branching Gram-positive filamentous bacteria of the oral flora. They cause chronic abscesses with draining sinuses and yellow sulfur granules, often in the jaw.
Engulfment of particles or microbes by a cell, forming a phagosome that fuses with a lysosome. Neutrophils, macrophages and dendritic cells do it, aided by opsonins like IgG and C3b.
Spirochetes transmitted by ticks and lice. Borrelia burgdorferi causes Lyme disease and Borrelia recurrentis causes relapsing fever.
Failure of the lower esophageal sphincter to relax because of loss of inhibitory myenteric neurons. It causes dysphagia to solids and liquids, with a bird's beak on barium swallow.
Abnormal aggregates visible in cell cytoplasm or nucleus, from viral infection or protein accumulation. Examples include Negri bodies in rabies and Lewy bodies in Parkinson disease.
A nucleoside made of thymine and deoxyribose, a building block of DNA. Thymidylate synthase makes its monophosphate, and this step is blocked by 5-fluorouracil.

A prostaglandin E1 analog that protects the gastric mucosa and causes uterine contraction. It is used for NSAID ulcer prevention and labor induction, and is contraindicated in pregnancy except for abortion.
A basic amino acid that is a urea cycle intermediate and the precursor of nitric oxide. It is made from citrulline and cleaved by arginase into ornithine and urea.
An aggressive neuroendocrine lung cancer of central location, linked to smoking. It has small blue cells, can secrete ACTH or ADH, and expresses neuron-specific enolase.
A nonselective beta-blocker used for hypertension, angina, migraine prophylaxis, essential tremor and thyrotoxicosis symptoms. It can cause bronchospasm, bradycardia and masks hypoglycemia.
The volume of plasma filtered by the kidney glomeruli per minute, normally about 100-125 mL/min. It is estimated from creatinine clearance and is the key measure of kidney function.
A peptide similar to PTH that binds the PTH receptor. Tumors, especially squamous cell carcinoma, secrete it to cause hypercalcemia of malignancy with low PTH.
An enzyme that interconverts creatine and phosphocreatine for muscle energy. Its MB isoform rises with myocardial infarction, and total levels rise with rhabdomyolysis.
Double vision, from misaligned eyes (as in cranial nerve III, IV or VI palsy) or lens/corneal problems. It resolves on covering one eye when the cause is misalignment.

The most common thyroid cancer, with Orphan Annie eye nuclei, nuclear grooves and psammoma bodies. It spreads to cervical lymph nodes, has a good prognosis, and is linked to RET/PTC and BRAF mutations and radiation.

Kidney damage from long-standing diabetes, causing proteinuria and progressive loss of function. Pathology shows glomerular basement membrane thickening and nodular mesangial sclerosis (Kimmelstiel-Wilson nodules).

A glassy, homogeneous pink material seen on histology, representing accumulated proteins. Examples include hyaline membranes in respiratory distress and hyaline arteriolosclerosis in hypertension and diabetes.
Noncancerous enlargement of the prostate's periurethral zone in older men, from stromal and glandular growth driven by DHT. It causes urinary hesitancy, weak stream and nocturia.
The ovarian structure formed from the ruptured follicle after ovulation. It secretes progesterone to support early pregnancy and regresses to the corpus albicans if no pregnancy occurs.
Bleeding anywhere in the digestive tract. Hematochezia (bright red blood per rectum) usually means lower bleeding, while melena and hematemesis point to upper sources.
Painful menstruation. Primary forms arise from prostaglandin-driven uterine contractions, while secondary forms result from endometriosis or adenomyosis.
Inflammation of the breast, usually infection during lactation by Staphylococcus aureus. It causes a red, tender, warm breast and fever.

Reduced gonadal function causing low sex hormones. Primary (hypergonadotropic) disease has high LH and FSH, while secondary (hypogonadotropic) disease has low LH and FSH from pituitary or hypothalamic problems.
Elevated pressure in the portal vein, usually from cirrhosis. It causes varices, ascites, splenomegaly and caput medusae through portosystemic shunting.
Prostaglandin E2 used to ripen the cervix and induce labor. It is also the PGE2 that causes fever and vasodilation, and is made via cyclooxygenase.

Antibiotics that block bacterial folate synthesis by inhibiting dihydropteroate synthase as PABA analogs. Adverse effects include hypersensitivity, hemolysis in G6PD deficiency and kernicterus in newborns.
Narrowing of the airways from contraction of bronchial smooth muscle. It occurs in asthma and with muscarinic or histamine stimulation, and is relieved by beta-2 agonists.
A class IA antiarrhythmic that blocks sodium channels and prolongs the QRS and QT. It is used in ventricular and supraventricular tachycardias and can cause drug-induced lupus.
An anthracycline chemotherapy that intercalates DNA and inhibits topoisomerase II. Its notable toxicity is dilated cardiomyopathy, partly prevented by dexrazoxane.
A collection of pus in a body cavity, most often the pleural space after pneumonia. It requires drainage and shows low pH and glucose in the fluid.
A cytokine from Th2 cells that promotes B-cell class switching to IgE and IgG and drives Th2 differentiation. It also induces macrophage alternative activation.
Cell junctions anchoring adjacent cells through cadherins linked to intermediate filaments. Autoantibodies against desmoglein cause pemphigus vulgaris.
Inadequate weight gain or growth in an infant or child, below expected percentiles. Causes include inadequate intake, malabsorption or chronic illness.
Rise in eye pressure when the iris blocks drainage at the anterior chamber angle. It presents with severe eye pain, halos, a fixed mid-dilated pupil and nausea, and is an emergency.
A urease-producing, swarming Gram-negative rod that causes urinary tract infections. Urea splitting alkalinizes the urine and forms struvite (staghorn) stones.

Toxicity from lead exposure, inhibiting ALA dehydratase and ferrochelatase in heme synthesis. It causes microcytic anemia with basophilic stippling, abdominal pain, neuropathy and lead lines on gums; treated with chelators.
The anterior part of the cerebrum for executive function, personality, motor planning and speech production (Broca area). Frontal eye fields drive voluntary gaze to the opposite side.
Inherited red cell membrane defect (ankyrin, spectrin or band 3) producing spherical cells that the spleen destroys. It causes hemolytic anemia with increased MCHC; treated with splenectomy.
A myeloproliferative neoplasm with the Philadelphia chromosome t(9;22), forming the BCR-ABL tyrosine kinase. It shows marked leukocytosis with left shift and is treated with imatinib.
The largest salivary gland, in front of and below the ear, with the facial nerve passing through it. Its duct (Stensen) opens opposite the upper second molar; mumps causes swelling.
An eating disorder of binge eating followed by compensatory purging or fasting. Repeated vomiting causes hypokalemic metabolic alkalosis, enamel erosion and Russell sign.
An ulcer in the first part of the duodenum, usually from H. pylori or NSAIDs. Pain often improves with meals, and a posterior ulcer can erode the gastroduodenal artery.

Recurrent unexpected panic attacks, abrupt episodes of intense fear with palpitations, sweating and dyspnea, followed by worry about further attacks. First-line treatment is SSRIs and cognitive behavioral therapy.

Pressure on the spinal cord from tumor, disc, abscess or trauma, causing weakness, sensory loss and bowel/bladder dysfunction. Conus medullaris syndrome affects the lowest cord, with early sphincter dysfunction.
A benzodiazepine that enhances GABA-A receptor chloride channel opening frequency. It treats anxiety, seizures and alcohol withdrawal and is safe in liver disease since it is glucuronidated.
Compression of the median nerve at the wrist, causing numbness and tingling of the thumb, index and middle fingers and thenar weakness. Tinel and Phalen signs are positive.
Fungal infection from inhaling Coccidioides spores in the southwestern US, producing respiratory illness or disseminated disease. Tissue shows spherules containing endospores.

Raised pressure within a closed fascial compartment, compromising blood flow and nerve function. It follows fracture or crush injury and presents with pain on passive stretch; treated with fasciotomy.
The main hormone secreted by the thyroid (T4), converted in tissues to active T3. Levothyroxine is its synthetic form, used to treat hypothyroidism.
Protozoa transmitted by insects. T. brucei (tsetse fly) causes African sleeping sickness and T. cruzi (reduviid bug) causes Chagas disease.
The process in which B cells, aided by helper T cells, become plasma cells that secrete antibodies against an antigen. It involves class switching and somatic hypermutation in germinal centers.
The ribosomal RNA enzyme (ribozyme) in the large subunit that forms peptide bonds between amino acids during translation. Chloramphenicol blocks it.
A viral enzyme that makes DNA from an RNA template. It is used by retroviruses such as HIV and is the target of nucleoside reverse transcriptase inhibitors.
Neuroendocrine cells of the adrenal medulla derived from neural crest. They secrete epinephrine and norepinephrine, and give rise to pheochromocytoma.
An ulcer in the stomach lining, from H. pylori or NSAIDs. Pain often worsens with meals, and it carries a risk of malignancy, unlike duodenal ulcers.
Excess growth hormone in adults, usually from a pituitary adenoma. It causes enlarged hands, feet, jaw and tongue, and raises IGF-1; also causes glucose intolerance and cardiomyopathy.
The clinical state of excess circulating thyroid hormone, causing weight loss, tremor, heat intolerance and tachycardia. Graves disease is the most common cause.
DNA wrapped around histone proteins in the nucleus. Loosely packed euchromatin is transcriptionally active, while tightly packed heterochromatin is silent.
The most common kidney stone type, forming envelope-shaped or dumbbell crystals. It is associated with hypercalciuria, Crohn disease and ethylene glycol poisoning.

Insulin resistance with relative insulin deficiency, causing chronic hyperglycemia. It is linked to obesity and treated with lifestyle change, metformin and other agents; amyloid deposits appear in pancreatic islets.
A hormone made mainly by peritubular interstitial cells of the kidney in response to hypoxia. It stimulates red cell production in marrow and is given in anemia of chronic kidney disease.
A remnant of the omphalomesenteric (vitelline) duct causing an outpouching of the ileum. It often has ectopic gastric tissue and can bleed.
A congenital aortic valve with two leaflets instead of three. It predisposes to aortic stenosis, regurgitation and ascending aortic dilation, and associates with Turner syndrome and coarctation.
A protein made by the fetal liver and yolk sac. High maternal levels suggest neural tube defects, while elevated adult levels suggest hepatocellular carcinoma or yolk sac tumor.
The phase of the cell cycle when DNA is replicated. It follows G1 and precedes G2, and antimetabolites such as methotrexate act here.
The most common colon cancer, a glandular malignancy arising from adenomatous polyps. It follows the APC, KRAS, p53 sequence, and CEA is used for monitoring.
An abnormally small head circumference with reduced brain size. Causes include Zika virus, fetal alcohol exposure, trisomy 13 and 18, and genetic disorders.
Impaired conduction of impulses from atria to ventricles. First-degree is a long PR interval, second-degree drops beats (Mobitz I or II), and third-degree has complete AV dissociation.
A hole in the wall between the ventricles, the most common congenital heart defect. It produces a holosystolic murmur and left-to-right shunt, and can reverse into Eisenmenger syndrome.
Breakdown of fibrin clots by plasmin, which is activated from plasminogen by tissue plasminogen activator. Alteplase uses this pathway to treat thrombosis.
A drug that binds tubulin and blocks microtubule assembly, reducing neutrophil migration. It treats acute gout and familial Mediterranean fever, with diarrhea as a common side effect.

A congenital heart defect with pulmonary stenosis, right ventricular hypertrophy, overriding aorta and a ventricular septal defect. It causes cyanosis with a boot-shaped heart; squatting relieves tet spells.
Fluid accumulating in the pericardial sac. Rapid or large collections cause tamponade, with hypotension, muffled heart sounds, jugular venous distension and pulsus paradoxus.
Bleeding into the subarachnoid space, commonly from a ruptured berry aneurysm. It causes a sudden severe thunderclap headache, with blood or xanthochromia in CSF.
Granulocytes with large basophilic granules containing histamine and heparin. They mediate allergic reactions and are increased in chronic myeloid leukemia.
An osmotic diuretic that is freely filtered and not reabsorbed. It reduces intracranial and intraocular pressure and is contraindicated in anuria and heart failure.
The volume of plasma reaching the kidneys per minute, about 600-700 mL/min. It is estimated by the clearance of para-aminohippuric acid (PAH).
Formation of stones in the kidney, causing colicky flank pain radiating to the groin with hematuria. Types include calcium oxalate, struvite, uric acid and cystine.

Inherited failure of both T and B cell function, causing recurrent severe infections, thrush and failure to thrive in infancy. Causes include IL-2R gamma chain defects and adenosine deaminase deficiency.
Pupillary dilation. It occurs with sympathetic stimulation or parasympathetic blockade, as with atropine or oculomotor nerve compression.
A specialized cell or nerve ending that converts a stimulus (touch, pain, temperature, light) into neural signals. Types include mechanoreceptors, nociceptors and thermoreceptors.
An ascending spinal pathway carrying pain and temperature (lateral) and crude touch (anterior). Fibers decussate in the anterior white commissure within a few levels of entering the cord.
Sharp, shooting pain along the distribution of a nerve. Examples include trigeminal neuralgia, relieved by carbamazepine, and postherpetic neuralgia.
A common benign tumor of arachnoid cap cells, attached to the dura. It shows spindle cells in whorls with psammoma bodies, and is more frequent in women and with NF2.
Growths protruding from the colon lining, including adenomatous (premalignant) and hyperplastic types. Villous and larger adenomas carry greater cancer risk.
Crystal arthritis from calcium pyrophosphate deposition, usually in the knee of older adults. Crystals are rhomboid and weakly positively birefringent; cartilage calcification is chondrocalcinosis.
A drug that blocks renal tubular organic acid transport. It raises levels of penicillin and treats chronic gout by increasing uric acid excretion.
Fungal infection from Blastomyces, acquired in the central and eastern US. It causes lung disease and skin or bone lesions, with broad-based budding yeast.
A Gram-variable coccobacillus linked to bacterial vaginosis. It causes thin gray discharge with a fishy odor and clue cells.
A lipopeptide antibiotic that inserts into Gram-positive cell membranes and depolarizes them. It treats MRSA and VRE bacteremia but is inactivated by surfactant and can cause myopathy.
A spore-forming anaerobic Gram-positive rod that causes pseudomembranous colitis after antibiotics. It produces toxins A and B and is treated with oral vancomycin or fidaxomicin.
Sudden loss of cardiac pumping with no circulation. Rhythms include ventricular fibrillation, pulseless ventricular tachycardia, asystole and pulseless electrical activity.

A severe mucocutaneous reaction, usually to drugs such as sulfonamides, allopurinol or anticonvulsants. It causes skin detachment and mucosal erosions; when over 30% of skin is involved it is toxic epidermal necrolysis.
Hypertrophy of the pyloric muscle in infants, causing projectile nonbilious vomiting at 2-6 weeks of age. An olive-shaped mass is palpable and labs show hypochloremic hypokalemic metabolic alkalosis.
A dopamine D2 antagonist and prokinetic that increases gastric emptying. It treats gastroparesis and nausea but can cause extrapyramidal effects and tardive dyskinesia.
A vascular tumor caused by HHV-8, common in AIDS patients. It presents as purple skin and mucosal plaques made of spindle cells.
A nucleoside reverse transcriptase inhibitor (AZT) used in HIV and to prevent perinatal transmission. Its toxicity is bone marrow suppression with anemia.
A protein with carbohydrate chains attached. Examples include antibodies, receptors and cell surface markers.
Natural alkaloids from the opium poppy (morphine, codeine) acting on mu, kappa and delta opioid receptors. Overdose causes respiratory depression and pinpoint pupils, reversed by naloxone.
Breakdown of glycogen to glucose-1-phosphate by glycogen phosphorylase, then to glucose. It is stimulated by glucagon and epinephrine.
The outer part of the adrenal gland, with three zones: glomerulosa (aldosterone), fasciculata (cortisol) and reticularis (androgens). It derives from mesoderm.
Loss of half of the visual field in each eye. Bitemporal loss suggests chiasm compression (pituitary tumor), while homonymous loss suggests a lesion behind the chiasm.
Increased water content in brain tissue. Vasogenic edema comes from blood-brain barrier breakdown (tumors), while cytotoxic edema comes from cell injury (ischemia).
The vein that carries nutrient-rich blood from the gut, spleen and pancreas to the liver. It forms from the superior mesenteric and splenic veins behind the pancreatic neck.
Finger-like projections of the cell membrane that increase absorptive surface, forming the brush border in the intestine and proximal tubule. They contain actin filaments.
The observable characteristics of an organism resulting from genotype and environment.
The weakest estrogen, produced in large amounts by the placenta during pregnancy. Low levels in the triple or quad screen suggest Down syndrome.
Abnormally heavy or prolonged menstrual bleeding (over 80 mL per cycle). Causes include fibroids, adenomyosis, coagulopathies and anovulation.

Dilation of the pampiniform venous plexus in the scrotum, feeling like a bag of worms. It is more common on the left because the left testicular vein drains into the renal vein, and can cause infertility.
A chronic skin disease causing white, thin, atrophic plaques in the vulvar or genital area. It causes itching and scarring and carries a small risk of squamous cell carcinoma.
The first stool of a newborn, dark green and sticky. Failure to pass it suggests cystic fibrosis or Hirschsprung disease, and in utero passage can cause aspiration syndrome.
Excess amniotic fluid. It is associated with maternal diabetes and fetal conditions that impair swallowing, such as esophageal atresia or anencephaly.
An agent that prevents and treats eclamptic seizures and treats torsades de pointes. Toxicity causes loss of deep tendon reflexes and respiratory depression, reversed by calcium gluconate.
An essential sulfur-containing amino acid that is the start codon amino acid in eukaryotes. It forms S-adenosylmethionine, the major methyl donor, and homocysteine.
Infection by Corynebacterium diphtheriae, whose toxin inhibits protein synthesis by ADP-ribosylating EF-2. It causes a gray pseudomembrane in the throat and bull neck.
The fluid pressure pushing water out of capillaries into tissue. With oncotic pressure it determines Starling forces; elevated venous hydrostatic pressure causes edema.
Unexpected death from cardiac causes within an hour of symptoms, usually from ventricular fibrillation. Causes include coronary disease, hypertrophic cardiomyopathy and long QT syndrome.
A protein on the hepatitis B virus envelope. Its presence in blood marks active infection or carrier state, while anti-HBs antibody marks immunity.

A medium-vessel vasculitis in children under 5. It causes prolonged fever, conjunctivitis, strawberry tongue, rash, swollen hands/feet and cervical lymphadenopathy, with coronary aneurysm risk; treated with IVIG and aspirin.
Insufficient blood flow to heart muscle, usually from coronary atherosclerosis, causing angina. Prolonged ischemia leads to infarction.
Restoration of blood flow to ischemic tissue. It can cause further injury through free radicals and calcium overload (reperfusion injury).
Dilation of the abdominal aorta to 3 cm or more, linked to atherosclerosis and smoking. Rupture causes pain, hypotension and a pulsatile mass; screening is by ultrasound in older male smokers.
A test that evaluates heart function under exertion or drug stress, to look for ischemia with ECG, echocardiography or imaging. It is used for suspected coronary artery disease.
Shock from failure of the heart to pump, most often after massive myocardial infarction. It causes hypotension with elevated wedge pressure, cold extremities and low cardiac output.
Chemotherapy drugs such as doxorubicin and daunorubicin that intercalate DNA and inhibit topoisomerase II. They cause dilated cardiomyopathy through free radicals.

A glomerular disease with thickened basement membranes and mesangial proliferation, giving a tram-track appearance. It causes nephrotic and nephritic features and is linked to hepatitis C and C3 nephritic factor.

A methylxanthine that inhibits phosphodiesterase and blocks adenosine receptors. It relaxes bronchial smooth muscle in asthma and COPD, but has a narrow therapeutic window with tachyarrhythmias and seizures.

Branches of the vagus nerve supplying the larynx. The recurrent laryngeal nerve moves all intrinsic muscles except cricothyroid, and the superior laryngeal nerve supplies cricothyroid and sensation above the cords.
A toxin that inhibits cytochrome c oxidase in the electron transport chain, blocking oxidative phosphorylation. It causes lactic acidosis and a bitter almond odor; treated with hydroxocobalamin.
